column1: Why does an oboist risk light-headedness while a flutist runs out of air quickly?
column2: Oboe requires high mouth pressure (20–40 cm H₂O) but very low air flow (5–12 L/min), so stale CO₂-rich air builds up; flute requires high air volume (20–40 L/min) at very low pressure, depleting air fast. Oboe/bassoon players should worry about CO₂ buildup, not running out of air; flute/sax players should worry about running out of air, not CO₂.

column1: What are the three muscle systems controlling woodwind breath, and what is each one's job?
column2: 1) Diaphragm — contracts/drops for inhalation (passive release on exhale). 2) Abdominal wall — squeezes inward/upward to actively drive controlled exhale ('breath support'). 3) Throat/glottis — must stay open and relaxed (like a yawn); tightening here is the #1 cause of airy, unfocused tone and fatigue.

column1: Describe the reed as a physical system and explain the Bernoulli-driven cycle that produces vibration.
column2: The reed is a cantilever clamped at the mouthpiece table, free at the tip. Fast air across the reed-mouthpiece gap drops in pressure (Bernoulli), sucking the tip closed; airflow stops, pressure rebuilds behind the reed, and the cane's springiness snaps it open again. Repeating hundreds of times per second produces tone.

column1: How does cane thickness and moisture affect reed response?
column2: Thin cane flexes easily, opening/closing fast — bright, free-blowing, but can be unstable. Thick cane resists flexing — dark, resistant, can be stuffy. Moisture softens the internal fiber matrix, shifting cane between these states.

column1: Name the five reed zones from base to tip and state which one should never be touched during adjustment.
column2: Heel/butt, vamp, heart, rails, tip — in order base to tip. The heel should never be touched; it anchors to the mouthpiece table, and unevenness there causes air leaks at the sides regardless of tip work.

column1: What is the single core invariant governing pitch control via fingering on any woodwind instrument?
column2: Opening a tone hole closer to the mouthpiece shortens the vibrating air column and raises the pitch — the open hole becomes the new end of the standing wave. This applies to both reed-driven and edge-tone (flute) instruments.

column1: Why does the clarinet overblow a twelfth instead of an octave, unlike flute and saxophone?
column2: The clarinet's chalumeau register is a cylindrical bore closed at the reed end, so only odd harmonics sound (fn = (2n−1)v/4L), producing a jump of a twelfth. Flute (cylindrical, open at both ends) and sax (conical, behaves like open-both-ends) ring with all harmonics (fn = nv/2L) and overblow an octave.

column1: At 120 BPM playing sixteenth notes, how much time does a finger-tongue coordination window actually leave for clean articulation?
column2: Each sixteenth note lasts 125 ms; the air column needs 20–50 ms to restabilize after a fingering change, leaving well under 100 ms to move fingers cleanly and lock pitch before the next tongue stroke. Clean articulation requires finger movement to complete within 2–5 ms of tongue release.

column1: What causes 'scooping' (pitch sliding at note onset) in woodwind articulation?
column2: Fingers are still moving when the tongue releases air, so the air column gets excited mid-transition between fingerings — a timing error, not an embouchure or air problem.

column1: What is 'motor chunking' and why is it the central payoff of finger-technique practice?
column2: Motor chunking is when a drilled fingering sequence (scale, arpeggio, trill) stops being separate finger decisions and becomes one pre-loaded motor program retrieved as a single unit. It is the biggest lever for technical fluency, since fingers have no independent muscles and rely on shared tendon/forearm control.

column1: List the four physical levers a woodwind player uses in real time to correct intonation, with their pitch direction.
column2: 1) Embouchure/lip pressure — firmer = sharp (±30–50 cents). 2) Jaw drop/relaxed corners — flat (±30–50 cents). 3) Tongue arch/throat shape — 'ee' = sharp, 'oh' = flat (±10–20 cents). 4) Air speed — faster = sharper on reeds, faster+lower angle = flatter on flute (±5–15 cents). Mechanical pull (barrel/bocal/headjoint) also flattens pitch when pulled out (±15–25 cents/mm).

column1: Why is the clarinet's throat register (G4–B♭4) notoriously flat and thin, and why are saxophone palm keys (D6–F6) sharp?
column2: Clarinet throat notes use a fingering/venting combination that is acoustically weak due to the cylindrical closed-reed-end bore, producing flat, thin tone that must be corrected with embouchure every time. Saxophone palm keys vent through small, indirect tone holes in the conical bore, which consistently makes them run sharp.
